title: Is Reselling Profitable in 2026? Fees, Margins and Taxes Explained
summary: Know the profitability of reselling, focusing on sourcing, expenses, and tax implications to maximize your earnings in the growing secondhand market.
body_markdown:
Yes, reselling is profitable for sellers who source strategically, understand marketplace fees, and consistently sell inventory for more than their total costs. However, making


*sales* doesn't necessarily mean making money…


Understanding your profit margins, expenses, and taxes is essential to building a profitable resale business. 💰


## Main Takeaways


- **Reselling is profitable in 2026** , but success depends on sourcing costs, marketplace fees, pricing, and consistent sales.


- **The secondhand market continues to grow.** The global secondhand apparel market is projected to reach $393 billion by 2030 according to


[ThredUp](https://www.thredup.com/resale) .


- **Marketplace fees impact profitability.** Selling fees, shipping expenses, packaging, and inventory costs all reduce your earnings.


- **Profit margins matter more than sales revenue.** A reseller generating thousands in sales isn't necessarily earning thousands in profit.


- **Reselling income may be taxable** , even if you don't receive a Form 1099-K. Keeping accurate records is essential.


- **Vendoo helps resellers maximize profitability** with Profit Tracking, Business Analytics, crosslisting, and automated inventory management.


## Is Reselling Profitable? The Short Answer


Yes! Reselling is profitable for sellers who buy inventory at the right price, understand their expenses, and consistently make sales.


There is significant demand for secondhand merchandise, particularly clothing and accessories. According to the


[ThredUp Resale Report](https://www.thredup.com/resale) , the global secondhand apparel market is projected to reach $393 billion by 2030, growing twice as fast as the overall apparel market.


The profits speak for themselves! Take a look at this seller’s 2026 year-to-date stats from Vendoo 👀


## What Eats Into Your Reselling Profit


Your reselling profit is what remains after subtracting the expenses associated with selling your inventory. Understanding these costs is essential because even high sales volume can produce disappointing profits when expenses aren't managed.


Here are the primary expenses resellers should consider:


- **Marketplace fees:** Most resale platforms charge fees when an item sells. Seller fees are generally a portion of the sale price. Some also charge listing fees, payment processing fees, or other expenses that affect your payout.

These are standard fees and may not include additional charges, promotional fees, or variations in how platforms calculate fees. For other platforms, including Poshmark, use the


[Vendoo Marketplace Fee Calculator](https://vendoo.co/marketplaces-fee-calculator) to estimate selling expenses.


- **Cost of goods (COG):** Your cost of goods is the amount you spend acquiring inventory.


- **Shipping and packaging:** Shipping labels, boxes, mailers, tape, tissue paper, and other packaging supplies cost money. If you offer free shipping, the shipping expense comes directly out of your earnings. Even inexpensive supplies add up across hundreds of orders.


- **Supplies and services:** Additional costs might include equipment, mileage, photo-editing software, crosslisting apps, laundry detergent, utilities, bookkeeping services, marketing and promotional costs, etc. These things can add up!


- **Your time:** Sourcing, cleaning, photographing, measuring, listing, communicating with buyers, and shipping orders all require time. An item generating $20 in profit isn't particularly impressive if you spent two hours working on it. Consider your effective hourly earnings alongside your profit per item.


## **How to Calculate Your Reselling Profit**


To calculate your reselling profit on a sale:


Start with your sale price, subtract your cost of goods, subtract your marketplace fees, and subtract seller-paid shipping.


Let's use these leggings that sold on Poshmark as an example.


**COG:** I purchased these leggings for $25.


**Sale Price** : They sold for $100 on Poshmark.


**Marketplace Fees:** Poshmark’s seller fee was $20 (10% of the sale price.


**Shipping Cost:** None to me, the seller (buyer paid shipping).


So, to calculate profit:


Sale Price ($100)


*minus* COG ($25)


*minus* Marketplace Fees ($20)


*equals* Profit ($55)


**Profit:** $55


**Don’t forget additional expenses.** While the profit of this


*item* is clear, there are routine expenses such as shipping supplies, software, and mileage to consider.


At the end of each month (or quarter), be sure to deduct all other costs against cumulative profit from all sales to ascertain true profitability.


💡


**Tip:** It's important to distinguish profit margin from return on investment (ROI). Profit margin measures how much of your sale price remains as profit, while ROI compares your profit to the amount invested.


## Is Reselling Worth It?


Reselling is worth it if you enjoy sourcing merchandise, can dedicate time to listing consistently, and are willing to track your expenses and earnings.


However, reselling isn't passive income. It requires ongoing work, and inventory doesn't always sell quickly.


#### **Reselling might be worth it if:**


- You enjoy shopping secondhand and researching resale value.


- You can consistently dedicate time to sourcing, photographing, listing, and shipping.


- You understand marketplace fees and can identify profitable inventory.


- You’re comfortable managing inventory and tracking financial performance.


- You’re willing to adjust your strategy based on sales data.


- You’re organized and self-motivated.


#### **Reselling might not be worth it if:**


- You don’t have time to manage listings and fulfill orders.


- You frequently purchase inventory without researching sold prices.


- You expect every item to sell immediately.


- You struggle to separate revenue from actual profit.


- Your inventory costs and business expenses consistently exceed your earnings.


Want to save time and maximize profit reselling?


## Ways to Increase Your Reselling Profit


Improving profitability doesn’t necessarily require selling more items. Sometimes, it means selling


*better* items, or making smarter decisions with your existing inventory. Here are some tips:


1. **Source smarter.** Research brands, styles, demand, and comparable sold prices before purchasing inventory. A low purchase price doesn’t automatically make something a good investment.


2. **Price based on sold listings.** Active listing prices show what sellers are asking. Sold listings provide a better indication of what buyers are actually paying.


3. **List on multiple marketplaces.** Crosslisting exposes your inventory to different audiences and increases opportunities to make sales without purchasing additional merchandise.


4. **Keep listings fresh.** Review stale inventory, update pricing, improve descriptions, and relist older merchandise when appropriate.


5. **Know your numbers.** Track average sale price, cost of goods, fees, and profit margins to identify which products generate the strongest returns.

## Reselling Taxes: Hobby vs. Business


You must


**report** all income, even if that income isn’t necessarily profit. Reselling income


*may* be taxable regardless of whether you consider yourself a casual seller, hobbyist, or business owner.


Understanding the distinction between hobby income and business income is important because the IRS treats them differently.


#### **Hobby or Reselling Business?**


According to the


[Taxpayer Advocate Service](https://www.taxpayeradvocate.irs.gov/news/tax-tips/hobby-vs-business-income/2026/03/) , the IRS considers several factors when determining whether an activity constitutes a business, including:


- Whether you operate with the intention of making a profit.


- Whether you maintain accurate financial records.


- How much time and effort you devote to the activity.


- Whether you’ve generated profits in previous years.


- Whether you conduct the activity in a businesslike manner.


No single factor automatically determines your classification. A reseller can operate a business without forming an LLC or selling full-time.


💡


**Tip:** Don’t just take it from us, speak to a licensed tax specialist in your state.


#### **Form 1099-K and Reselling Income**


For federal reporting purposes, online marketplaces generally must issue Form 1099-K when payments exceed the annual threshold (currently $20,000) and/or involve more than 200 transactions during the calendar year.


However,


**the Form 1099-K threshold is a reporting requirement, not a tax-free income allowance.**


You are likely required to report taxable reselling income even if you never receive a Form 1099-K.


💡


**Tip:** Learn more directly from the


[IRS guidance on Form 1099-K](https://www.irs.gov/businesses/understanding-your-form-1099-k) .


**Keep Accurate Records**


Resellers should maintain records of inventory purchases, sales, marketplace fees, shipping expenses, refunds, and any other business costs.


Accurate bookkeeping makes it easier to calculate profits, prepare tax returns, and substantiate business expenses.


For more information, Check out our


[Bookkeeping for Resellers](https://blog.vendoo.co/book-keeping-for-resellers) guide.


Remember, tax obligations depend on your individual circumstances, so consult a qualified tax professional for advice about reporting income, deductible expenses, and business classification.
